name: ksqlDB
license: Confluent Community License (source-available, not OSI open source); Apache 2.0 until December 2018
summary: Confluent’s SQL server for Kafka: queries that run forever, turning topics into new topics and into tables you can look up.
intro: ksqlDB is a server, or a group of servers, that sits next to a Kafka cluster. You declare a `STREAM` or a `TABLE` over an existing topic and write SQL. A persistent query (`CREATE STREAM AS SELECT` or `CREATE TABLE AS SELECT`) is compiled into a Kafka Streams application that runs in the background on the servers, writing its results to a new topic and, for tables, keeping them in local state stores. Clients then ask in two ways: a push query (`EMIT CHANGES`) holds a connection open and streams every change, while a pull query returns the current value for a key and closes, like a database lookup. Servers with the same `ksql.service.id` share the work, and in interactive mode they agree on the statements to run through an internal command topic. ksqlDB can also run Kafka Connect connectors, embedded or on an existing Connect cluster.

The code is on GitHub under the Confluent Community License: you may use, change and redistribute it, but not offer it as a hosted service that competes with Confluent. The last standalone release, 0.29.0, came out in June 2023; ksqlDB now ships as part of Confluent Platform and as a managed service in Confluent Cloud, billed per Confluent Streaming Unit (CSU) per hour in clusters of 4 to 28 CSUs. For new work, Confluent Cloud’s docs now recommend its Flink service; ksqlDB “remains fully supported for existing applications”. Confluent has been part of IBM since March 2026.
strengths: Stream processing in SQL: filters, joins and windowed aggregations over Kafka topics without writing Java
Tables you can query: a pull query answers a key lookup from state kept up to date as events arrive
Push queries stream every change to a client over one long-lived HTTP connection
Runs on Kafka Streams, so it inherits its local state stores, changelog backups and exactly-once mode
Can create and manage Kafka Connect connectors, such as a JDBC source, from the same SQL
limits: Not open source: the Confluent Community License forbids running it as a competing hosted service
Winding down: no standalone release since 0.29.0 (June 2023), and Confluent points new Confluent Cloud work to Flink
Pull queries are key lookups by default; scans need a setting, and the docs warn of deadlocks under many concurrent pull queries
Confluent Cloud limits: no user-defined functions, 40 persistent queries per cluster, no Enterprise clusters, and resizing goes through support
Kafka only: every source and result is a Kafka topic, and each persistent query adds internal topics and local state

snippet.title: A stream, a table kept up to date by a persistent query, then pull and push queries
source: -- register a stream over a topic (created with 6 partitions if missing)
CREATE STREAM pageviews (user_id VARCHAR KEY, page VARCHAR)
-- persistent query: runs on the servers and keeps this table current
-- pull query: the value right now, then the query ends
SELECT views FROM views_per_user WHERE user_id = 'u-42';
-- push query: stay connected and receive every change
SELECT user_id, views FROM views_per_user EMIT CHANGES;
-- views per user per one-minute window

sections.title: Ways to run it in 2026
sections.intro: The same engine comes in three forms, and only two of them still get releases.

items.name: Standalone ksqlDB
items.text: The `confluentinc/ksqldb-server` image and the docs at docs.ksqldb.io. The last release was 0.29.0 in June 2023. The GitHub repository still gets fixes and dependency updates, but on Confluent Platform branches.

items.name: Confluent Platform
items.text: Ships as `cp-ksqldb-server`, versioned with the rest of the platform (7.x and 8.x lines in 2026). The code stays under the Confluent Community License; longer support comes with a paid Confluent Platform subscription.

items.name: Confluent Cloud
items.text: Managed clusters of 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 or 28 CSUs; 8 CSUs or more get high availability. Prices vary by cloud and region and are shown in the console. Supported for existing apps, with Flink recommended for new ones.

story: Kafka Streams made stream processing a library, but you still had to write Java. In August 2017 Confluent co-founder Neha Narkhede announced KSQL, “a streaming SQL engine for Apache Kafka”, as a developer preview. A query such as counting errors per one-minute tumbling window became a `CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT` statement, which KSQL turned into a Kafka Streams application that ran indefinitely.

KSQL started under Apache 2.0. In December 2018, Jay Kreps moved it and other Confluent components to the new Confluent Community License: the code could still be downloaded, changed and redistributed, but “you cannot create a KSQL-as-a-service offering”, a rule aimed at cloud providers. In November 2019 a release “so significant that we’re giving it a new name” became ksqlDB. It added pull queries, which read the current value from a materialized table, and connector management, so one system could ingest, process and serve data.

Confluent then bet on Apache Flink. It agreed to buy Immerok, a managed Flink start-up, in January 2023, and made Flink generally available in Confluent Cloud in March 2024. ksqlDB’s last standalone release, 0.29.0, came out in June 2023. IBM completed its acquisition of Confluent on 17 March 2026.

choices.choice: SQL compiled to Kafka Streams, not a new engine
choices.why: KSQL reused Kafka Streams’ partitioning, local state and fault tolerance, so a SQL statement became an ordinary Streams application and Confluent didn’t have to build a second runtime.

choices.choice: Streams and tables as SQL objects
choices.why: They map directly onto Kafka Streams’ `KStream` and `KTable`: a stream is a sequence of facts, a table the latest value per key.
Applications need both a live feed of changes and request-and-response lookups. Serving lookups from the state stores saves copying results into a separate database.
Confluent wanted to keep cloud providers from selling KSQL as a service while leaving the code free for everyone else to use, change and embed.

timeline.text: KSQL announced as a developer preview in August
Moves from Apache 2.0 to the Confluent Community License in December
Renamed ksqlDB, adding pull queries and connector management
Confluent agrees to buy Immerok for Flink; last standalone release, 0.29.0
Flink becomes generally available in Confluent Cloud
IBM completes its acquisition of Confluent in March
